english: I came to buy a SIM card
usage: I came to buy a SIM card
Polite; said as you walk into a phone shop or convenience store
I'm here to get a SIM
반말, only with a friend tagging along, not to staff
Straight request once you know they have it
선불 ('prepaid') vs. 후불 ('postpaid') — ask which they sell
examples: 유심 사러 왔어요.
I came to buy a SIM card.
Opening line as you reach the counter; 사러 왔다 = came in order to buy
외국인인데 유심 사러 왔어요. 여권 보여 드릴까요?
I'm a foreigner, I came for a SIM — should I show my passport?
Offering your 여권 up front speeds things up; ID is required for 유심 registration
A: 어서 오세요. 뭐 찾으세요? / B: 선불 유심 사러 왔어요. 여행용으로요.
A: Welcome! What can I help you with? / B: I came to buy a prepaid SIM — for travel.
A/B exchange: give 선불 ('prepaid') and your purpose so staff can pull the right product immediately
nuance: 유심 is the Korean pronunciation of 'USIM', the subscriber identity chip — Koreans almost never say 'SIM 카드' with both English words; the single word 유심 is standard everywhere from street kiosks to carrier shops. The grammar pattern is verb-stem + -(으)러 ('in order to') + 왔어요 ('came'), literally 'I came in order to buy', which is the natural way to state your purpose on entering any shop. This purpose-statement form 사러 왔어요 is distinct from 유심 하나 주세요 (the direct purchase request): use 사러 왔어요 first as your opening, then switch to 주세요 once stock is confirmed. Crucially, 유심 (the physical chip) and 개통 (activating the line) are two separate steps — buying a 유심 does not automatically mean your number is live. Default 존댓말 with staff in all situations; 반말 사러 왔어 is only possible between peers.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I came in order to buy a USIM.' 실제: a natural shop-entry purpose statement, not a description of movement. The -(으)러 왔어요 frame is how you announce WHY you walked in; it does NOT imply you searched for a store — it simply declares intent.

Used at the counter of a carrier shop (SKT, KT, LG U+), a convenience store kiosk, or an airport SIM stand. Always 존댓말 (유심 사러 왔어요) to staff. 반말 유심 사러 왔어 is only between friends — never to employees. Foreigners should add 외국인인데요 ('I'm a foreigner') to flag the ID requirement immediately.

유심 하나 주세요 ('one SIM please') is the direct purchase request. The dividing line: 사러 왔어요 opens the conversation and invites the staff to guide you, while 주세요 finalises the transaction. Use 사러 왔어요 first, 주세요 after they confirm stock or show you options.
선불 유심 사러 왔어요 (prepaid SIM), 데이터 유심 사러 왔어요 (data-only SIM), 유심 바꾸러 왔어요 (came to swap/replace a SIM). 바꾸러 왔어요 is the variant when you already have a phone and just need a new chip.

Two traps: (1) saying 유심 카드 살 수 있어요? — this checks your own ability/permission and sounds like a hesitant question rather than a confident opener; use the purpose form 사러 왔어요 instead. (2) Dropping the particle as 유심을 사러 왔어요 is fine, but many learners add 을 when it should be dropped in natural speech — 유심 사러 왔어요 with no particle is more fluent.

mistakes: Saying 유심 카드 (sim-card) as two English words.
Koreans say just 유심. Adding '카드' is redundant and sounds learner-ish. Use 유심 하나 주세요 or 유심 사러 왔어요.
Asking 유심 살 수 있어요? to open.
That literally checks your ability/permission to buy. To state your purpose on entering, say 유심 사러 왔어요; to order, 유심 하나 주세요.
Confusing 유심 with 개통.
유심 is the physical chip; 개통 is activating the phone line. Buying a 유심 doesn't automatically mean 개통 — you may still need to ask them to 개통해 주세요.

english: I came to activate my phone
usage: Polite; the standard opener at a carrier shop
I'm here to set up my phone
반말, only with a friend, never to staff
Could you activate it for me?
Direct request once you're at the desk
I'm looking to activate a new line
examples: 개통하러 왔어요.
I came to activate a phone.
Said at the counter of an SKT/KT/LG U+ shop; the first thing out of your mouth
유심 샀는데 개통하러 왔어요.
I bought a SIM and came to activate it.
Sequence matters: you have the 유심, now you need 개통 to make the number live
A: 어떻게 오셨어요? / B: 외국인 등록증으로 개통할 수 있어요? 개통하러 왔어요.
A: How can I help you? / B: Can I activate with my ARC? I came to set up service.
A/B exchange: staff open with 어떻게 오셨어요?; answer by stating your purpose and flagging the ID you have
nuance: 개통 (開通) literally means 'opening through' — the moment a phone number goes live and can send/receive calls and data. The -(으)러 왔어요 frame ('came in order to') declares your purpose at the shop door, just as with 유심 사러 왔어요. Default 존댓말 always. The critical distinction: 개통 is the technical activation of the LINE, while 가입 (加入) is enrolling as a subscriber to a carrier/plan — you do both at once when starting fresh, but staff treat them separately: they'll ask about 요금제 (your plan) and 약정 (contract term) before they can 개통. Do not say 폰 켜러 왔어요 ('I came to power the phone on') — 켜다 turns a screen on, not a number live. Also, the formal English 'set up' does NOT map to 설정; 설정 is for in-phone settings menus. Foreigners must bring 외국인 등록증 (ARC) or 여권, as 개통 legally requires ID registration.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I came in order to open-through (activate).' 실제: a shop opener that declares your exact purpose — activating a phone line so calls and data work. 개통 is the industry word for the moment a number goes live; it is not casual shorthand but the precise technical term used on all forms.

Used at a carrier store (SKT, KT, LG U+) counter or sometimes by phone/online. Always 존댓말 to staff; 반말 개통하러 왔어 is only peer-to-peer. Be prepared for staff to ask 요금제는 어떻게 하실 건가요? (which plan?) before they can complete 개통. Have your ID and method of payment ready.

새로 개통하려고요 ('I'm looking to set up a new line') is the nearest softened variant — the ending -려고요 states intent rather than announcing arrival, making it slightly less direct than 개통하러 왔어요. The dividing line: 개통하러 왔어요 is a purposive shop-entry opener (you physically arrived to do this); 새로 개통하려고요 is more tentative, used when you're still exploring options on the phone or not yet committed. Use 왔어요 at the counter; -려고요 when calling ahead or browsing online.

새로 개통하러 왔어요 (new activation), 재개통하러 왔어요 (re-activate after a suspension), 번호 이동 개통하러 왔어요 (activate while porting a number). Adding 외국인인데요 before the request immediately signals you may need an ARC check.

Two major traps: (1) 폰 켜러 왔어요 — 켜다 means powering the device screen on, not activating a number; 개통 is not 켜기. (2) 셋업하러 / 설정하러 왔어요 — 설정 is navigating phone settings menus; for registering a phone line the only word is 개통. A third: over-translating 'set up' as 설정 is extremely common among English speakers and will confuse staff.

mistakes: Saying 폰 켜러 왔어요 to mean activate service.
켜다 is to power the device ON (the screen). Activating the line/number is 개통: say 개통하러 왔어요.
Using 셋업하러 / 설정하러 왔어요.
셋업/설정 sound like configuring phone settings, not registering a line. The right word for going live is 개통.
Confusing 개통 with 가입.
가입 is becoming a subscriber (joining a plan/carrier); 개통 is the line being switched on. Mention 요금제 if you also need to pick a plan, since 개통 alone doesn't choose one.

usage: Polite; hand the choice to the staff
반말, to a friend who knows carriers
Asking specifically for the budget option
Is there a plan that fits me?
Asking them to match a plan to your usage
examples: 데이터 많이 쓰는데, 요금제 추천해 주세요.
I use a lot of data — could you recommend a plan?
State your usage profile first so staff can narrow down immediately; 데이터 많이 쓰다 is the key signal
통화는 거의 안 하고 데이터만 써요. 요금제 추천해 주세요.
I barely call, I only use data — please recommend a plan.
Contrast 통화 (calls) vs. 데이터 to guide their suggestion; eliminating calls lets them skip voice-heavy plans
A: 어떤 요금제 찾으세요? / B: 잘 모르겠어요. 한 달에 5만 원 이하로 요금제 추천해 주세요.
A: What kind of plan are you looking for? / B: I'm not sure. Could you recommend a plan under 50,000 won a month?
A/B exchange: when uncertain, give a budget ceiling — 5만 원 이하 — so staff can filter immediately
nuance: 요금제 (料金制) means the monthly bundle — the specific combination of data, calls, and texts at a fixed price that you select when subscribing. 추천해 주세요 is 추천하다 (推薦, 'recommend') restructured as the favor form: verb-stem + 해 + 주세요. This favor form is essential — it asks them to DO it FOR you and signals you genuinely want guidance, not just a menu listing. Without the 해, 요금제 추천 주세요 is ungrammatical (you cannot 'give' a recommendation). And 요금제 추천하세요 without 주세요 is an imperative that sounds bossy. Default 존댓말 in all carrier contexts. The key vocabulary contrast: 요금제 is the recurring monthly plan, 약정 is the contract commitment length, and 기기값/단말기 is the phone hardware price — staff will address each separately, so knowing the boundary prevents confusion. Never say 플랜 here; Koreans use 요금제 exclusively in this context.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Please do the action of recommending a plan for me.' 실제: a genuine request for staff expertise, not just a question — using 해 주세요 signals you want them to decide, which in Korean service culture prompts a real consultation rather than just handing you a brochure.

Said at a carrier shop, on a phone consultation call, or in a 카카오 chat with a carrier agent. Always 존댓말. To get a precise recommendation, add usage context first: 한 달에 데이터 얼마나 쓰세요? is what they'll ask back, so preempt it with 데이터 많이 써요 or 통화 거의 안 해요.

저한테 맞는 요금제 있어요? ('Is there a plan that suits me?') is nearly identical in intent but frames the question as 'does one exist for me?' — it's slightly more passive. 요금제 추천해 주세요 actively solicits expert judgment. Use 추천해 주세요 when you want to be guided; 맞는 요금제 있어요? when you want options laid out.
제일 싼 요금제 추천해 주세요 (cheapest plan), 무제한 요금제 중에 추천해 주세요 (recommend among unlimited plans), 어르신 요금제 추천해 주세요 (senior plan). Adding a budget cap — 5만 원 이하로 — sharpens the request.

Three traps: (1) 플랜 추천해 주세요 — Koreans say 요금제, not 플랜. (2) 요금제 추천 주세요 — ungrammatical; you cannot 'give' a recommendation. (3) 요금제 추천하세요 — an imperative that sounds like a command to a superior. Always 해 + 주세요.

mistakes: Saying 플랜 추천해 주세요.
The English 'plan' (플랜) is unnatural here. The word for a phone plan is 요금제: 요금제 추천해 주세요.
Saying 요금제 추천하세요 to staff.
Bare 추천하세요 is a command ('recommend!') and sounds bossy. Use the favor form 추천해 주세요, asking them to do it for you.
Confusing 요금제 with 약정.
요금제 is the monthly plan (data/calls); 약정 is the contract length you commit to. They're separate — asking about a plan doesn't settle how long you're locked in.

usage: Set me up with unlimited data
반말, to a friend helping you pick
I'll go with the unlimited plan
Announcing your own choice at the counter
Checking first whether they offer it
examples: 유튜브 많이 봐서 데이터 무제한으로 해 주세요.
I watch a lot of YouTube, so make it unlimited data.
Give the reason first — 유튜브 많이 보다 — so staff understand why unlimited is the right fit
완전 무제한이에요, 아니면 속도 제한 있어요?
Is it truly unlimited, or is there a speed cap?
Many 무제한 plans throttle after a daily threshold; 완전 무제한 means no throttle at all — always ask
A: 요금제 고르셨어요? / B: 네, 데이터 무제한으로 해 주세요. 완전 무제한 맞죠?
A: Have you chosen a plan? / B: Yes, please make it unlimited data. It's fully unlimited, right?
A/B exchange: confirm 완전 무제한 before committing — throttled and true unlimited have the same label in many shops
nuance: 무제한 (無制限) literally means 'no restriction/limit', and 데이터 무제한 is the unlimited-data option. The structure is [desired state] + -(으)로 + 해 주세요: the particle -(으)로 marks a result or mode you want to apply ('set it AS unlimited'), and 해 주세요 is the favor-request form. This -(으)로 is indispensable — it selects the option, the same way you say 뜨겁게 해 주세요 ('make it hot') or 조용히 해 주세요 ('keep it quiet'). The real-world danger is that 무제한 alone does not guarantee full speed: many plans branded as 무제한 throttle to 1 Mbps after a daily cap, while 완전 무제한 or 속도 제한 없는 무제한 means genuinely unrestricted. Always ask 완전 무제한이에요? before signing. 무제한 is not a verb; the action is 해 주세요, and the particle -(으)로 does the work of 'set it as'.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Please make it [into] unlimited data.' The particle -(으)로 is the key: it selects a mode or result, so 무제한으로 해 주세요 = 'please configure it AS the unlimited option.' This structure recurs across all option-selection requests in Korean service settings.

Said when selecting a plan at a carrier counter, on a phone with a carrier agent, or in a chat window. Always 존댓말 to staff. Before using this phrase, it is strongly advised to first ask 데이터 무제한 요금제 있어요? to confirm the option exists at your chosen price tier.

무제한 요금제로 할게요 ('I'll go with the unlimited plan') makes the SAME choice but frames it as YOUR decision rather than a request for the staff to set it up. 해 주세요 invites them to process the selection; 할게요 announces it as your conclusion. Both are natural; 할게요 is slightly more decisive.
완전 무제한으로 해 주세요 (truly unlimited, no throttle), 속도 제한 없는 걸로 해 주세요 (the one with no speed limit), 데이터 무제한 중 제일 싼 걸로 해 주세요 (cheapest unlimited plan). The variant 완전 무제한 is the one that protects you.

Two traps: (1) 데이터 무제한을 해 주세요 — the object particle 을 is wrong here; you are selecting a mode with -(으)로, not acting on an object. (2) Assuming any plan called 무제한 is truly unrestricted — Korean marketing often uses 무제한 for throttled plans; only 완전 무제한 or 속도 제한 없음 guarantees full speed.

mistakes: Saying 데이터 무제한을 해 주세요.
When picking a setting you use -(으)로, not the object 을. Correct: 데이터 무제한으로 해 주세요 ('set it up as unlimited').
Assuming 무제한 always means full speed.
Many 무제한 plans throttle after a daily cap (속도 제한). For no slowdown, confirm 완전 무제한이에요? before committing.
Treating 무제한 as a verb: 무제한해 주세요.
무제한 is a noun/state, not an action. Attach -(으)로 해 주세요: 데이터 무제한으로 해 주세요.

english: Can I use it without a contract?
usage: Can I use it without a contract?
Polite; asking to avoid being locked in
반말, to a friend who's done it before
무약정 = the no-contract option, stated as your wish
How many months is the contract?
Asking the term length if a contract is required
examples: 한국에 오래 안 있어서 약정 없이 쓸 수 있어요?
I'm not in Korea long — can I use it without a contract?
오래 안 있다 ('not staying long') is the classic justification; give the reason first to help staff suggest an appropriate option
약정 없이 쓰면 요금이 더 비싸요?
If I go without a contract, is the fee higher?
무약정 usually means no phone subsidy, so the monthly cost or device price is often higher — confirm before deciding
A: 약정 기간은 24개월인데요. / B: 약정 없이 쓸 수 있어요? 무약정으로 하고 싶어요.
A: The contract period is 24 months. / B: Can I use it without a contract? I'd like to go contract-free.
A/B exchange: staff state the default term; you push back with 약정 없이 and the cleaner request 무약정으로 하고 싶어요
nuance: 약정 (約定) is the commitment period — typically 24 months — during which you promise to stay with the carrier, usually in exchange for a phone subsidy or plan discount. 약정 없이 쓸 수 있어요? uses 없이 ('without') + 쓸 수 있어요? ('can I use?') to ask for the no-commitment option. The dedicated compound word is 무약정 (無約定), so 무약정으로 하고 싶어요 is the crisp, unambiguous request. The decisive contrast: 약정 is the COMMITMENT LENGTH, not the plan itself (요금제). Changing a 요금제 mid-contract is usually possible; ending the 약정 early triggers a 위약금 (違約金, early-termination penalty) proportional to the remaining months. Choosing 무약정 typically removes the device subsidy, so the phone may cost full price — that tradeoff is why people ask 약정 없이 쓰면 더 비싸요?. Do not say 계약 없이; 계약 is general legal-contract language and sounds out of place in this carrier context.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Can I use (the service) without a commitment period?' 실제: a request to avoid being locked into a multi-month contract that would charge a 위약금 if you leave early. 약정 없이 쓰다 is about freedom to leave, not about choosing a cheaper plan per se.

Said at a carrier shop counter when the staff mentions a default 24-month 약정. Always 존댓말 to staff. This question is especially important for foreigners who may leave Korea before the 약정 ends; pair it with a cost check: 약정 없이 하면 얼마예요?

무약정으로 하고 싶어요 is the positive statement of what you want (cleaner, more direct). 약정 없이 쓸 수 있어요? is a question checking feasibility. Use the question when you're unsure the option exists; use the statement when you've confirmed it and want to select it.
무약정으로 해 주세요 (direct request), 약정 없는 요금제 있어요? (asking if a no-contract plan exists), 위약금 없이 해지할 수 있어요? (can I cancel without a penalty?). 무약정 is the compressed key word.

Two traps: (1) 계약 없이 — 계약 is the broad legal word for any written contract; phone-industry commitment is called 약정. Staff may understand 계약, but the term sounds wrong in a carrier shop. (2) Expecting 무약정 to cost the same — it almost never does, because carriers subsidize phones via contracts; always ask 더 비싸요? when going 무약정.

mistakes: Using 계약 instead of 약정.
계약 is the general word for 'contract' and sounds off for phone plans. The carrier term is 약정 (commitment); no-contract is 무약정.
Thinking 약정 and 요금제 are the same.
요금제 is the monthly plan; 약정 is how long you're locked in. You can switch plans, but ending 약정 early incurs a 위약금 (penalty).
Expecting 무약정 to cost the same as a contract plan.
Contracts usually subsidize the phone. 무약정 ('no contract') often means no device discount, so ask 약정 없이 쓰면 더 비싸요?

usage: Polite; asking the data allowance of a plan
반말, to a friend comparing plans
기가 ('giga/GB') — the most concrete way to ask
What happens when I use it all up?
Asking about overage / throttling after the cap
examples: 이 요금제 데이터 몇 기가예요? 영상 많이 봐요.
How many gigs of data does this plan have? I watch a lot of video.
기가 is unambiguous; stating 영상 많이 봐요 lets staff flag whether that allocation is realistic for you
데이터 다 쓰면 속도 느려져요, 아니면 추가 요금이에요?
When I run out, does it slow down, or is there an extra charge?
속도 느려지다 (throttle) vs. 추가 요금 (overage fee) are two very different outcomes — know which applies before you commit
A: 이 요금제 데이터 얼마예요? / B: 오십 기가예요. 다 쓰면 속도 제한 있어요.
A: How much data does this plan have? / B: Fifty gigabytes. There's a speed limit once you use it up.
A/B exchange: shows the natural follow-up — staff answer in 기가 and immediately clarify the post-cap policy
nuance: 데이터 얼마예요? uses 얼마 ('how much'), which normally asks price — so the question is mildly ambiguous: it could mean 'how much does data cost?' or 'how much data is included?'. In context (when you're pointing at a plan), staff understand it as the allowance, but the sharper, unambiguous version is 데이터 몇 기가예요? using 기가 (GB). Koreans count gigabytes with Sino-Korean numbers: 십 기가 (10 GB), 삼십 기가 (30 GB), 오십 기가 (50 GB) — never 열 기가 or 서른 기가 with native Korean numerals. An equally important follow-up is 다 쓰면 ('once it's all used'): data plans in Korea frequently throttle speed after the cap rather than charging an overage, so asking 속도 느려져요? vs. 추가 요금 있어요? reveals which applies. Default 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'How much is the data?' — but 얼마 is the price word, so the intent is read from context. 실제: in a plan-comparison conversation the meaning is the data ALLOWANCE. To be unambiguous, say 몇 기가예요? ('how many gigabytes?') which uniquely asks amount, not price.

Said when comparing two or three plans at a carrier counter, or on a carrier's website/chat. 존댓말 (얼마예요?) with staff; 반말 (얼마야?) with a peer. To avoid any ambiguity, always anchor with 데이터 before 얼마예요 — a lone 얼마예요? on its own will be heard as asking the plan's PRICE.

데이터 몇 기가예요? is the precise sibling expression: it asks amount only, never price. The dividing line: 데이터 얼마예요? can be heard as a price question depending on tone; 데이터 몇 기가예요? can only be about the allowance size. Use 기가 when you want zero ambiguity.
일별 데이터 몇 기가예요? (how many GB per day?), 하루 데이터 얼마나 써요? (how much do I use per day?) — useful if the plan has a daily cap. Counting: 십 기가, 이십 기가, 삼십 기가, 오십 기가, 백 기가.

Two traps: (1) 데이터 얼마나 많아요? ('how plentiful is the data?') — this sounds like a comment on quantity rather than a request for a spec; use 몇 기가예요?. (2) Counting with native numbers — 열 기가, 스물 기가 — is wrong; 기가 takes Sino-Korean numerals: 십, 이십, 삼십.

mistakes: Expecting 데이터 얼마예요? to clearly ask the amount.
얼마 often means 'how much (money)'. To unambiguously ask the data size, say 데이터 몇 기가예요?
Saying 데이터 얼마나 많아요?
That sounds like 'how plentiful is it?' rather than asking the spec. Ask the figure: 데이터 몇 기가예요?
Counting gigs with native numbers (열 기가).
기가 takes Sino-Korean numbers: 십 기가 (10GB), 오십 기가 (50GB) — not 열/쉰 기가.

english: How do I verify my identity?
usage: How do I verify my identity?
Polite; asking how to pass identity verification
How do I do the ID check?
반말, asking a friend walking you through it
The identity verification won't go through
Can foreigners do identity verification too?
Asking if the system accepts non-Koreans
examples: 휴대폰 본인 인증이 자꾸 안 돼요. 외국인인데 어떻게 해요?
Phone identity verification keeps failing — I'm a foreigner, how do I do it?
휴대폰 본인 인증 (SMS-based ID check) frequently fails for foreigners whose Korean number isn't linked to a 주민번호; state 외국인인데 to get the alternative path
외국인 등록증 번호로 본인 인증 할 수 있어요?
Can I verify with my ARC number?
ARC (외국인 등록증) number is the standard alternative for foreigners when phone-based 본인 인증 fails
A: 본인 인증 어떻게 해요? 앱에서 막혀요. / B: 휴대폰 인증 말고 아이핀이나 외국인 등록증으로 해 보세요.
A: How do I verify my identity? I'm stuck in the app. / B: Try using I-PIN or your ARC instead of phone verification.
A/B exchange: shows the common real-world block and the practical alternatives — 아이핀 (I-PIN) and 외국인 등록증 번호
nuance: 본인 (本人) means 'oneself / the person in question' and 인증 (認證) means 'authentication' — together they describe the ubiquitous Korean requirement to prove you are who you claim before accessing any online service, signing up for anything, or completing a purchase. 어떻게 해요? asks the procedure. This is NOT the same as 로그인 (logging into an existing account) or 가입 (creating one); 본인 인증 is the legal identity layer on top. The most common method is 휴대폰 본인 인증 (a verification SMS to your registered phone), but this channel is tied to the Korean national ID system and routinely fails for foreigners — the alternative paths are 아이핀 (a government-issued internet ID number) and 외국인 등록증 번호 (ARC number). The complaint form is 본인 인증이 안 돼요 ('the verification won't go through') using 되다 for 'function/work'. Say 신원 확인 only in official/police contexts; in everyday digital life the set phrase is 본인 인증.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'How do I do oneself-authentication?' 실제: a practical question about which button, number, or document unblocks a Korean website or service that demands ID proof. The verification is not optional — it's hard-coded into most Korean apps and government portals.

Said to carrier staff, a 고객센터 (call center) agent, or a bank clerk when the digital flow stalls. Also typed into help-chat windows. Always 존댓말 in service contexts. The most important accompanying phrase is 외국인인데요 — flagging your status immediately routes staff to the alternative verification options.

본인 인증이 안 돼요 ('identity verification won't go through') is the nearest near-synonym expression — it shifts from a how-to question to a failure report. The dividing line: 본인 인증 어떻게 해요? asks for the procedure before you have tried; 본인 인증이 안 돼요 reports that a specific attempt has failed and you need an alternative path. In practice foreigners often find themselves moving from the first phrase to the second within minutes of starting the enrollment flow.
본인 인증이 안 돼요 (not working), 본인 인증 다시 해야 해요? (do I need to re-verify?), 본인 인증 넘어가는 법 알아요? (do you know how to get past the verification?). The fixed noun phrase is always 본인 인증; don't split it.

Two traps: (1) 신원 확인 — this is police/official documentation language, not what you say to an app or customer service agent. The everyday digital term is 본인 인증. (2) 본인 인증 안 해요 ('I don't verify') implies a choice you're making; the form for 'it won't work' is 안 돼요, using 되다, not 하다.

mistakes: Saying 신원 확인 instead of 본인 인증.
신원 확인 is an official/police-style 'identity check'. For app and website verification, the set term is 본인 인증.
Confusing 본인 인증 with 로그인.
로그인 just signs into an existing account; 본인 인증 proves your identity, often required additionally. They're separate steps.
Saying 본인 인증 안 해요 to mean it's failing.
안 해요 means 'I don't do it' (a choice). For 'it won't work', use 되다: 본인 인증이 안 돼요.

english: I'd like to get Wi-Fi installed
usage: I'd like to get Wi-Fi installed
I want to get Wi-Fi set up
반말, talking it over with a friend/roommate
I'd like to apply for internet installation
인터넷 설치 + 신청 ('apply') is the formal phrasing
I'd like to have new Wi-Fi put in
깔다 ('to lay/install') is the casual native verb
examples: 이사 와서 인터넷 설치 신청하려고요.
I just moved in and want to apply for internet installation.
이사 와서 ('having just moved in') is the most common trigger for this request; 신청 signals you want to open a formal order
와이파이 설치하려면 뭐가 필요해요? 외국인인데요.
What do I need to get Wi-Fi installed? I'm a foreigner.
설치하려면 ('if I want to install') checks requirements upfront; foreigners may need ARC for the service contract
A: 뭐 도와드릴까요? / B: 집에 와이파이 설치하고 싶은데요. 제일 빠른 게 뭐예요?
A: How can I help you? / B: I'd like to get Wi-Fi installed at home. What's the fastest option?
A/B exchange: use 설치하고 싶은데요 as the soft opener, then follow up immediately with your priority — speed, price, or availability date
nuance: 와이파이 here is a colloquial stand-in for home broadband internet — Koreans use it loosely to mean the router-plus-connection, even though technically 와이파이 is just the wireless signal from a 공유기 (router) and 인터넷 is the actual broadband line. 설치하다 (設置) + -고 싶어요 is the polite want-statement. The formal process word is 신청 ('application/request'): 인터넷 설치 신청하려고요 signals you want to open an official order, whereas 설치하고 싶어요 states a general wish. The casual, very natural native verb is 깔다 ('to lay down/install'): 와이파이 깔고 싶다 is everyday speech. The critical error is 와이파이 사고 싶어요 ('I want to buy Wi-Fi') — you don't buy the signal, you have the service installed or apply for it (설치/신청). Also, for home internet always anchor it as 집에 와이파이 so staff don't think you're asking about a café hotspot. The technician visit (기사님) requires someone to be home.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I want to install Wi-Fi.' 실제: a request to open a home-internet service contract and schedule a technician visit. In practice this means ordering a broadband line (인터넷) from KT, SKT, LG U+, or a cable provider — 와이파이 is used loosely for the whole package.

Said on a call to a carrier's 고객센터, at a carrier shop, or through an online application form. 존댓말 with agents. Always add 집에 ('at home') to scope it as home internet, not a public network. The next step after stating this wish is 설치 신청 and scheduling a 기사님 visit.

인터넷 설치 신청하려고요 is the formal, process-oriented version. The dividing line: 와이파이 설치하고 싶어요 expresses your desire; 인터넷 설치 신청하려고요 initiates the application. On a call center line, the second form moves things forward faster.
와이파이 깔고 싶은데요 (casual spoken variant), 인터넷 빨리 설치해 주세요 (please install it quickly), 이 아파트에 설치 돼요? (is installation possible in this apartment?). 깔다 is the go-to casual verb.

Two traps: (1) 와이파이 사고 싶어요 — you cannot 'buy' Wi-Fi the way you buy an item; use 설치하다 or 신청하다. (2) 셋업하러 왔어요 — 셋업 sounds like configuring a device, not ordering a service. Use 설치 신청 for starting a new home internet contract.

mistakes: Saying 와이파이 사고 싶어요.
You don't 'buy' Wi-Fi. You have it installed or apply for service: 와이파이 설치하고 싶어요 / 인터넷 설치 신청하려고요.
Using only 와이파이 without context for home internet.
와이파이 alone can mean a public hotspot. For home service anchor it: 집에 와이파이 설치하고 싶어요, or say 인터넷 설치.
Treating 설치하다 and 깔다 as different services.
Both mean 'install'. 설치하다 is neutral/formal, 깔다 is casual spoken ('와이파이 깔다'). Same request, different register.

english: When does the installation technician come?
usage: Polite (honorific 오세요); asking the visit time
반말, only when relaying to a friend, not to the agent
Could you come in the morning?
Requesting a morning slot for the visit
examples: 기사님 오시면 제가 집에 있어야 돼요?
Do I need to be home when the technician comes?
있어야 돼요 ('have to be there') — confirming you must be present; answer is almost always yes
내일 오전에 설치 기사님 오실 수 있어요?
Can the technician come tomorrow morning?
Pin a specific slot: 내일 오전 ('tomorrow morning'); time-slot requests use the verb-honorific form 오실 수 있어요?
A: 설치 기사님 언제 오세요? / B: 모레 오후 2시에 오실 예정이에요. 연락 드릴게요.
A: When does the installation technician come? / B: The technician is scheduled to come day after tomorrow at 2 p.m. We'll call you.
A/B exchange: models the typical call-center exchange — you ask, they give a date/time plus 연락 드릴게요 ('we'll call you')
nuance: 기사 (技士) means a skilled worker — technician, mechanic, or driver — and 님 is the honorific that elevates the title. In Korea you unfailingly add 님 and use subject-honorific verb endings (오시다, not 오다) when referring to any service worker coming to your home. The verb shift is the core grammar: from your perspective waiting at home, the 기사님 COMES TO you, so use 오다 ('come'), not 가다 ('go') — 가다 would be from the company's perspective. The distinction between 기사님 언제 오세요? (scheduling the PERSON's visit) and 설치 언제 가능해요? (asking when the SERVICE is available) is practical: the first pins a human arrival time, the second asks about the earliest booking. The typical call-center response gives a date and adds 연락 드릴게요 or 전화 드릴게요 ('we'll call you'), meaning the 기사님 will call ahead — confirm whether that's 당일 (the same day) or the night before.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'When does the installation technician come (honorific)?' 실제: scheduling a home visit. The honorific verb 오세요 (from 오시다) is not optional or overly formal — it is the neutral, expected way to speak about a 기사님 visiting your home.

Said on the phone with a carrier's 설치 예약 (installation booking) team, or in a chat. Always 존댓말 — and always subject-honorific (오세요/오시다), because you are referring to the 기사님 as the subject of the verb. Dropping 님 or using plain 와요 reads as rude toward a person doing work at your home.

설치 언제 돼요? / 설치 언제 가능해요? asks when the installation SERVICE is available — one step removed from the person. The dividing line: 기사님 언제 오세요? is about the human visit time; 설치 언제 가능해요? is about slot availability. Ask the second to find a window, then the first to confirm the appointment.
기사님 몇 시에 오세요? (what time?), 기사님 오시기 전에 연락 주세요 (please call before coming), 기사님 빨리 와 주실 수 있어요? (can you come sooner?). The subject-honorific 오시- is the constant across all variants.

Two traps: (1) 기사 언제 와요? — omitting 님 and using the plain 와요 is rude. A service worker visiting your home is always 기사님 ... 오세요. (2) 언제 가요? using 가다 — from your vantage point (home), the technician COMES TO YOU (오다). 가다 would only be correct if you were the company dispatching the worker.

mistakes: Saying 기사 언제 와요? (no 님, plain verb).
It's rude to a service worker. Add the honorific: 기사님 언제 오세요? — 님 plus the subject-honorific 오시-.
Calling them 테크니션 / 엔지니어.
The natural Korean is 기사님. It covers installers, repair techs, and even drivers — use it, not the English loanwords.
Using 가다 instead of 오다 from your view.
From you (waiting at home), the technician 'comes' to you: 오세요. 가다 ('go') would be from the company's side, not yours.

hangul: 기존 번호 그대로 쓸 수 있어요?
english: Can I keep my existing number?
usage: 기존 번호 그대로 쓸 수 있어요?
Can I keep my existing number?
Polite; asking to port/retain your number
Can I keep the same number?
반말, to a friend who switched carriers
I want to do a number transfer (port)
번호 이동 = porting your number to a new carrier
Quick check on whether the number stays
examples: 통신사 바꾸는데 번호 그대로 쓸 수 있어요?
I'm changing carriers — can I keep my number?
통신사 바꾸다 ('change carrier') is the porting scenario; stating it upfront tells staff which of the three enrollment types you want
번호 이동하면 요금이 더 싸져요?
If I port my number, does the fee get cheaper?
번호 이동 sometimes unlocks switching promotional discounts — worth asking
A: 신규 가입이세요, 번호 이동이세요, 기기 변경이세요? / B: 번호 이동이요. 기존 번호 그대로 쓸 수 있죠?
A: Is this a new signup, a number port, or a device upgrade? / B: Number port. I can keep my existing number, right?
A/B exchange: the staff's first question is always this three-way classification; answer 번호 이동 and confirm 그대로 in one move
nuance: 기존 (旣存) means 'existing/current' and 그대로 ('just as it is, unchanged') is the key adverb — together they ask to KEEP the number exactly as-is when switching carriers. This is formally called 번호 이동 ('number portability/MNP'). Every carrier shop will open a new enrollment by asking which of three paths you want: 번호 이동 (port existing number to new carrier), 기기 변경 (same carrier, new handset), or 신규 가입 (new number, new subscriber). Choosing the wrong category causes significant paperwork delays. Porting typically has no downtime — the number stays live throughout — but confirm there's no 공백 (gap in service). The natural expression 번호 유지할 수 있어요? ('can I maintain the number?') is understood but slightly stiff; 번호 그대로 쓸 수 있어요? is warmer and more conversational. Default 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Can I use the existing number as it is?' 실제: a request to port your phone number from your current carrier to a new one without it changing — what the industry calls 번호 이동 (MNP). 그대로 ('as-is') is the nuance word: it emphasises no modification at all.

Said at a new carrier's shop when signing up or on a phone call to the new carrier's 가입 team. Always 존댓말. The context trigger is always 통신사 바꾸다 ('changing carrier') — if you're staying with the same carrier and just getting a new phone, this question doesn't apply; that's 기기 변경.

번호 이동하고 싶어요 is the formal request that initiates porting and tells staff exactly what process to run. The dividing line: 기존 번호 그대로 쓸 수 있어요? is a feasibility question ('is it possible?'); 번호 이동하고 싶어요 is a declaration ('I want to do it'). Use the question when you're unsure, the statement when you've confirmed the option.
번호 이동으로 해 주세요 (please process it as a port), 기존 번호 유지하고 싶어요 (slightly more formal), 번호 바뀌지 않죠? (the number won't change, right? — confirmation tag). 그대로 can be swapped for 유지해서 in more formal speech.

Two traps: (1) 같은 번호 쓸 수 있어요? is understandable but 그대로 쓸 수 있어요? ('can I use it as-is?') more naturally captures the idea of an unchanged carry-over. (2) Confusing 번호 이동, 기기 변경, and 신규 가입 — staff will ask which one; choosing the wrong category at the start means restarting the paperwork.

mistakes: Saying just 같은 번호 쓸 수 있어요?
It's understandable, but the natural phrase is 번호 그대로 쓸 수 있어요?, and the formal action is 번호 이동 (porting).
Confusing 번호 이동 with 신규 가입.
번호 이동 keeps your existing number while switching carriers; 신규 가입 gives you a brand-new number. Specify which you want.
Mixing up 번호 이동 and 기기 변경.
번호 이동 = change carrier, keep number. 기기 변경 = same carrier, new phone. They are different processes — say the right one.

english: I've used up all my data
usage: I've used up all my data
Polite; explaining you're out of data
I'd like to add more data
데이터 추가 = buying a data top-up
examples: 데이터 다 썼어요. 어떻게 충전해요?
I've used up all my data — how do I top up?
충전 ('charging/topping up') is the prepaid refill action; follow the problem statement with the practical question
데이터 다 써서 속도가 너무 느려요. 추가 요금이 얼마예요?
I used up my data so the speed is really slow — how much is the extra?
Shows the consequence 속도 느리다 (throttled) and pivots to 추가 요금 ('overage/add-on fee') to restore full speed
A: 왜 인터넷이 이렇게 느려요? / B: 데이터 다 썼어요. 데이터 충전하거나 추가 요금 내야 할 것 같아요.
A: Why is the internet this slow? / B: I used up all my data. I think I need to top up or pay an extra fee.
A/B exchange: diagnose the slow connection and offer both fix options — 충전 or 추가 요금
nuance: 다 썼어요 is 다 ('all') + 썼어요 (past of 쓰다, 'to use') — 'I used all of it up.' The plain past tense marks completion: you consumed the entire allocation. Default 존댓말 to carrier staff; 반말 다 썼어 between friends. A close synonym is 데이터 다 떨어졌어요, using 떨어지다 ('to drop away/run out') — this frames the data as having depleted on its own rather than being consumed by you, which feels slightly less self-blaming and is equally natural. The post-depletion fix depends on your plan type: for prepaid (선불) you 충전 ('recharge a balance'), for postpaid plans with a data cap you 추가 ('add an extra data pack') or 요금제를 바꾸다 ('switch to a bigger plan'). The English-speaker pitfall is 데이터 끝났어요 — 끝나다 is for events ending (a class, a film), not a resource being depleted. Another is 데이터 없어요, which implies you never had data, not that you've exhausted it.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I used all the data.' 실제: reporting that your monthly data allocation is exhausted and your connection is now throttled or cut. The past completion 다 썼어요 signals the state is current — it happened and the effect is ongoing.

Said to carrier staff on the phone, in a chat window, or texted to a friend. 존댓말 with staff (다 썼어요); 반말 with peers (다 썼어). This statement almost always leads to a follow-up action, so pair it with 어떻게 충전해요? or 데이터 추가하고 싶어요 immediately.

데이터 다 떨어졌어요 ('the data has all dropped/run out') is nearly interchangeable. The slight dividing line: 다 썼어요 implies you consumed it actively; 다 떨어졌어요 frames depletion as something that happened to the data. Both are idiomatic; 떨어졌어요 is often preferred in texting as it sounds less like self-blame.
데이터 거의 다 됐어요 (almost used up), 데이터 한 기가 남았어요 (one GB left), 데이터 충전하고 싶어요 (want to top up). The progression: 거의 다 됐어요 → 다 썼어요 → 데이터 없어요 (completely gone, nothing at all).

Two traps: (1) 데이터 끝났어요 — 끝나다 is for events finishing (a movie, a class, a meeting), not resources being depleted; use 다 썼어요 or 다 떨어졌어요. (2) 데이터 없어요 — this means there is NO data on your plan at all; 다 썼어요 specifically means you HAD data and exhausted it.

mistakes: Saying 데이터 끝났어요.
끝나다 is for events ending (a class, a show), not a resource being depleted. Say 데이터 다 썼어요 or 데이터 다 떨어졌어요.
Saying 데이터 없어요 when you mean you used it up.
없어요 ('there is none') sounds like you never had data. To say you exhausted it, use 다 썼어요.
Confusing 충전 and 추가.
충전 = top up / refill a (prepaid) balance; 추가 = buy an additional data pack on top. Use the one matching your plan type.

usage: Polite; asking for the hotspot password
반말 + 비번 (slang for 비밀번호), very casual
Checking first whether Wi-Fi is available
Asking which network to connect to
examples: 여기 와이파이 비밀번호 뭐예요? 영수증에 있어요?
What's the Wi-Fi password here? Is it on the receipt?
Many cafés and restaurants print the 비밀번호 on the 영수증 (receipt) or post it on the wall — check there first before asking
와이파이 이름이 여러 개인데 어떤 거예요?
There are several Wi-Fi names — which one is it?
When multiple SSIDs appear in the list, ask 어떤 거 (which one) along with the password
A: 저기요, 와이파이 비번 뭐예요? / B: 영수증 뒷면에 있어요. 0410이요.
A: Excuse me, what's the Wi-Fi password? / B: It's on the back of your receipt — it's 0410.
A/B exchange: shows the real-world café interaction; 비번 is natural, not rude, in this casual public setting
nuance: 비밀번호 (祕密番號) literally means 'secret number' and is the standard Korean word for any password — Wi-Fi, bank PIN, or app login. In casual speech, Koreans routinely shorten it to 비번, making 와이파이 비번 뭐예요? perfectly natural and not at all impolite — it is simply informal register. Default 존댓말 (뭐예요) to café or guesthouse staff; 반말 뭐야 only among close peers. Two things to ask in cafés: 와이파이 이름이 뭐예요? (which SSID/network name to select) and 비밀번호 뭐예요? (what to type) — you need both if multiple networks are visible. The word 패스워드, though borrowed from English, sounds foreign and overly technical here; 비밀번호 / 비번 is the everyday Korean word. Also, 비밀번호 is for the password you type to join a network; 인증 번호 is a one-time verification code for signups — never conflate them.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'What is the secret number?' 실제: asking for the password to connect to a Wi-Fi network — the most natural and direct phrasing in Korean. In casual contexts 비번 replaces 비밀번호 without any loss of politeness provided the verb ending stays polite (뭐예요?).

Said at café counters, guesthouse check-ins, friends' homes, and offices. 존댓말 뭐예요? to staff; 반말 뭐야? to friends. In cafés check the 영수증 (receipt) or look for a posted sign first — asking when it's posted saves face. Korean café passwords are often the shop's phone number or a simple 4–8 digit sequence.

와이파이 이름이 뭐예요? is the SSID question; 비밀번호 뭐예요? is the password question. The dividing line: you need the SSID to pick the right network, then the 비밀번호 to unlock it. When multiple networks show up in your Wi-Fi list, always ask for both.

와이파이 비번 혹시 알아요? (do you happen to know the Wi-Fi password? — politely tentative), 비밀번호가 틀렸어요 (the password is wrong/not working), 와이파이 비번 바뀌었어요? (did the Wi-Fi password change?). 비번 is the go-to casual contraction.

Two traps: (1) 패스워드 — while understood, it sounds foreign; the native word is 비밀번호/비번. In cafés and homes, always say 비번. (2) 와이파이 코드 — 코드 is not used for Wi-Fi passwords in Korean; 비밀번호 is. Do not mix up 비밀번호 (static network password) with 인증 번호 (one-time code for account verification).

mistakes: Saying 패스워드 or 와이파이 코드.
The native word is 비밀번호 (or casual 비번). 패스워드 sounds foreign and 코드 isn't used for Wi-Fi: 와이파이 비밀번호 뭐예요?
Confusing 비밀번호 with 인증 번호.
비밀번호 is the Wi-Fi password; 인증 번호 is a one-time verification code (for signups). They're different — don't ask for the wrong one.
Mixing up the network name and password.
와이파이 이름 (SSID) is which network to join; 비밀번호 is what unlocks it. If several networks show, ask both: 이름이 뭐예요? and 비밀번호 뭐예요?

usage: Polite; reporting an outage to support
끊기다 ('to get cut off') for intermittent drops
Reporting slowness rather than a full outage
examples: 갑자기 인터넷이 안 돼요. 공유기 다시 켜 봤는데도 안 돼요.
The internet suddenly stopped — I tried restarting the router and it's still not working.
공유기 (router) + 다시 켜다 ('turn on again') = reboot; saying 봤는데도 ('I tried but') tells support you've already done the first-line fix
어제 설치했는데 인터넷이 안 돼요.
I had it installed yesterday but the internet doesn't work.
어제 설치했는데 ('installed yesterday but…') flags a brand-new setup issue, prompting support to check the activation, not just troubleshoot the router
A: 인터넷이 안 돼요. 어떻게 해야 해요? / B: 공유기 전원 껐다가 다시 켜 주시고, 그래도 안 되면 다시 연락 주세요.
A: The internet isn't working. What should I do? / B: Please turn the router off and back on, and if it's still not working, contact us again.
A/B exchange: models the standard support call — you report, they give the first-step 공유기 재부팅 instruction
nuance: 인터넷이 안 돼요 is 인터넷 + 이 (subject particle) + 안 돼요 (negative of 되다, 'to work/function'). 되다 is the essential Korean verb for things working or coming about, so 안 돼요 = 'it doesn't work' — the universal complaint formula for any service or machine failure. The subject particle 이/가 is mandatory because 되다 is intransitive; saying 인터넷을 안 돼요 with the object 을 is a common learner error. Three levels of complaint: 안 돼요 (completely down), 끊겨요 (intermittent drops, 끊기다 = to be cut off), 느려요 (slow but connected) — using the precise one tells the technician exactly what to investigate. Default 존댓말 to support staff. The phrase 인터넷이 일 안 해요 ('the internet isn't doing work') is a literal English-calque error; Korean machines and services are described with 되다, not 일하다. The troubleshooting sequence in Korea: reboot the 공유기 (router) first, then the 모뎀, then call 고객센터.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'The internet does not function.' 실제: a service-failure report using 되다 ('to work/function'), the standard Korean verb for anything that should be operating but isn't. The structure 이/가 + 안 돼요 is the template for ALL service-failure complaints in Korean.

Said to a carrier's 고객센터, to a guesthouse receptionist, or texted to a roommate. 존댓말 (안 돼요) with staff and strangers; 반말 (안 돼) with peers. Be ready to answer: 언제부터요? (since when?), 공유기 껐다 켰어요? (did you reboot the router?), and 컴퓨터인지 핸드폰인지요? (is it the computer or the phone?).

와이파이가 끊겨요 ('the Wi-Fi keeps cutting out') is the nearest near-synonym expression — it uses 끊기다 ('to be severed/disconnected') rather than 되다. The dividing line: 인터넷이 안 돼요 means the connection is completely dead and nothing loads at all; 와이파이가 끊겨요 means intermittent drops — you briefly connect, then lose signal, and reconnect. Support diagnoses these very differently: 안 돼요 typically triggers a line-level investigation or technician dispatch, while 끊겨요 points to a router, interference, or signal issue.
인터넷이 갑자기 안 돼요 (suddenly stopped), 인터넷이 가끔 끊겨요 (keeps cutting out), 인터넷이 하루 종일 안 됐어요 (hasn't worked all day). All use the 이/가 + 안 돼요 frame.

Three traps: (1) 인터넷을 안 돼요 — 되다 is intransitive; the subject particle 이/가 is required, never the object 을. (2) 인터넷이 일 안 해요 — 일하다 ('to work/labor') is for people, not machines; services 'work' as 되다. (3) 인터넷이 깨졌어요 — 깨지다 means physically shattered; for service failure use 안 돼요.

mistakes: Saying 인터넷을 안 돼요 with object 을.
되다 ('to work') takes the subject particle 이/가, not the object 을. Correct: 인터넷이 안 돼요.
Saying 인터넷이 일 안 해요.
Don't personify it as 'not doing work'. A non-working service is 안 돼요: 인터넷이 안 돼요.
Using 안 돼요 for intermittent drops.
안 돼요 means fully down. If it cuts in and out, say 끊겨요 (끊기다); if just slow, 느려요. The right word guides the fix.

usage: Is there a separate installation fee?
Confirming nothing more is added on
examples: 설치할 때 추가 요금 있어요? 설치비요.
Is there an extra charge for installation — the install fee?
Pin down the specific concern — 설치비 — so the agent can give a precise yes/no rather than a general overview
부가세 포함이에요, 아니면 추가 요금 있어요?
Is VAT included, or is there an added charge?
부가세 (VAT) is frequently added on top of the listed price in Korea — always confirm 포함이에요? before agreeing to a total
A: 한 달에 4만 원이에요. / B: 부가세나 추가 요금 있어요? 다 합치면 얼마예요?
A: It's 40,000 won per month. / B: Is there VAT or any extra charges? What's the total all-in?
A/B exchange: shows how to push past the headline price to the real all-in total — 다 합치면 얼마예요?
nuance: 추가 (追加) 요금 (料金) = an additional charge beyond the headline price, and 있어요? ('is there?') makes it a yes/no check. This is essential protective language in Korean phone and internet contracts, where 설치비 (installation fee), 부가세 (VAT), 위약금 (early-termination penalty), and 가입비 (sign-up fee) are common line items not included in the advertised 요금. Default 존댓말. The two-sided approach: 추가 요금 있어요? checks for surprises ('is anything extra?'); 다 포함이에요? / 다 해서 얼마예요? ('is everything included?' / 'how much all together?') arrives at the same goal from the positive side — ask both to triangulate the true total. The vocabulary contrast: 요금 is for recurring or service fees; 가격 is for the one-time price of an item (like the phone itself). Saying 숨은 요금 있어요? ('hidden fee?') is a literal translation trap — Koreans say 추가 요금 있어요? or 다른 비용 있어요?

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Is there an additional fee?' 실제: a protective question targeting the gap between the advertised price and what actually appears on the bill. In Korea the gap is common — 부가세 (10% VAT), 설치비, and 가입비 can all be off the headline figure.

Said at a carrier shop, during a phone consultation, or while reviewing an online plan comparison. 존댓말 with agents. The question works best when you name the specific fee you suspect: 설치비 있어요? 부가세 포함이에요? The targeted version gets a faster answer than the broad version.

다 포함이에요? ('Is everything included?') is the mirror image — it asks whether nothing is excluded rather than whether something extra exists. The dividing line: 추가 요금 있어요? puts the burden on staff to disclose extras; 다 포함이에요? puts the burden on them to confirm completeness. Both protect you; use them together for maximum coverage.
다른 비용 있어요? (any other costs?), 다 해서 얼마예요? (how much all-in?), 세금 포함이에요? (is tax included?), 위약금은요? (what about the early-termination penalty?). 다 해서 얼마예요? is the most direct all-in price check.

Two traps: (1) 숨은 요금 있어요? ('hidden fee?') is a literal English calque that sounds odd in Korean — say 추가 요금 있어요? or 다른 비용 있어요?. (2) Confusing 요금 (recurring service fee) with 가격 (item price) — for phone plans and services use 요금; for the handset's price say 기기값 or 폰 가격.

mistakes: Saying 숨은 요금 있어요? as a calque of 'hidden fee'.
That's a literal translation. Koreans ask 추가 요금 있어요? or 다른 비용 있어요? to surface extra costs.
Confusing 요금 with 가격.
요금 is a recurring service charge/fee; 가격 is an item's price. For monthly plans and installs, use 요금/비; for the phone's sticker, 기기값.
Assuming the quoted price includes VAT.
부가세 (VAT) is often added on top. Confirm with 부가세 포함이에요? ('is VAT included?') or ask 추가 요금 있어요?

english: How much of my contract is left?
usage: How much of my contract is left?
Quick check whether it's already expired
Asking the exact end date of the term
examples: 약정 기간이 얼마나 남았어요? 지금 해지하면 위약금 나와요?
How much contract is left? If I cancel now, is there a penalty?
The real-world two-part check: remaining time + the cost of leaving; 위약금 나오다 means a penalty 'comes out/is charged'
약정 끝나면 요금이 더 싸져요?
When the contract ends, does the fee get cheaper?
약정 끝나다 ('contract ends') sometimes lowers the monthly bill once the device subsidy is paid off — worth confirming
A: 약정 기간이 얼마나 남았어요? / B: 한 6개월 남으셨어요. 지금 해지하시면 위약금이 있어요.
A: How much of my contract is left? / B: About six months. If you cancel now, there will be a penalty.
A/B exchange: shows the typical support response — remaining months stated, penalty flagged
nuance: 약정 기간 is 약정 (約定, 'commitment') + 기간 (期間, 'period'), and 얼마나 남았어요? is 얼마나 ('how much') + 남았어요 (past of 남다, 'to be remaining'). 남다 is an intransitive verb: its subject takes 이/가, so the phrase is 기간이 얼마나 남았어요, never 기간을. The central weight of this question is its financial consequence: if any 약정 remains and you 해지 (cancel), a 위약금 (違約金, early-termination penalty) is calculated on the remaining months — so asking about 약정 remaining is really asking 'how much will it cost me to leave?' The pair of questions 얼마나 남았어요? (how much time remains, a span) and 언제 끝나요? / 언제까지예요? (when does it end, a specific date) cover the same ground from different angles. Default 존댓말. Watch tense: 약정 끝났어요? (has the contract already ended?) is past and checks if it's over; 언제 끝나요? is future-pointing and asks when it will end.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'How much of the contract period has remained?' 실제: a financial risk assessment — the remaining months determine the 위약금 you'll owe if you leave early. This question is almost always followed by 지금 해지하면 위약금 얼마예요? to calculate the exit cost.

Said on the phone with a carrier's 고객센터 or in the carrier app's account page. 존댓말 with agents. The question often precedes a decision to switch carriers (번호 이동) or upgrade a phone (기기 변경), so have your account details ready — staff will ask for your number and 본인 인증 before answering.

언제까지가 약정이에요? / 약정 언제 끝나요? asks the specific END DATE rather than the remaining duration. The dividing line: 얼마나 남았어요? gives you a duration to plan around (e.g., 'I have 6 months left'); 언제 끝나요? gives you a calendar date to aim for. Both are useful; the first is more practical for penalty calculations.
약정 몇 개월 남았어요? (how many months are left?), 약정 끝나려면 얼마나 걸려요? (how long until the contract ends?), 약정 만료되면 연락 주세요 (please contact me when the contract expires). 남다 is the key verb across all variants.

Two traps: (1) 약정 얼마나 왼쪽에 있어요? — 'left' as 'remaining' is expressed by 남다, not the directional 왼쪽. (2) Tense confusion: 끝났어요? ('has it ended?') is past; 언제 끝나요? ('when will it end?') is future-oriented. Choosing the wrong tense asks the wrong question — you may be told 'yes, it ended' when you meant to ask 'when does it end?'

mistakes: Translating 'left' as 왼쪽 (the direction).
'Remaining' is 남다, not 왼쪽 ('left side'). Say 약정 기간이 얼마나 남았어요?
Saying 약정 기간을 남았어요.
남다 ('to remain') takes the subject particle 이/가. Correct: 약정 기간이 얼마나 남았어요?
Forgetting 약정 ties to 위약금.
Canceling before the 약정 ends usually triggers a 위약금 (penalty). Pair the question with 지금 해지하면 위약금 나와요? to learn the real cost of leaving.

english: I'd like to cancel my service
usage: 반말, to a friend, not to the agent
Stating your purpose on a support call
How much is the cancellation penalty?
Asking the early-termination fee before canceling
examples: 인터넷 해지하고 싶은데요.
I'd like to cancel my internet, please.
The -는데요 ending softens the request, functioning like 'I'd like to…' — it opens the topic and invites the agent to respond rather than landing as a blunt demand
다음 달에 출국해서 해지하고 싶은데요. 위약금 있어요?
I'm leaving the country next month, so I'd like to cancel. Is there a penalty?
출국하다 ('to leave the country') is the most common reason foreigners 해지; attaching 위약금 있어요? in the same breath shows you know the rules
A: 해지하고 싶은데요. 약정이 아직 남았어요. / B: 위약금이 발생할 수 있어요. 확인해 드릴까요?
A: I'd like to cancel — my contract still has time left. / B: There may be a cancellation penalty. Would you like me to check?
A/B exchange: shows the realistic support exchange — you open with 해지하고 싶은데요, they flag the 위약금 risk and offer to calculate it
nuance: 해지 (解止) is the precise legal and industry term for terminating an ongoing contract or subscription — phone line, internet, streaming service, anything with a recurring commitment. The soft ender -는데요 on 해지하고 싶은데요 ('I would like to, but…') gently introduces the topic and invites the agent's response; it is warmer and less confrontational than the blunt 해지해 주세요 ('please terminate'). Default 존댓말 always. The triple contrast every learner needs: 해지 (cancel an ongoing CONTRACT) vs. 취소 (取消, cancel a one-time ORDER before it's processed) vs. 환불 (還拂, get a refund of money already paid). You 해지 a phone plan, 취소 a restaurant reservation, 환불 a defective product — using 취소 for a phone contract is noticeable. Also, 해지 (permanently end the service) vs. 정지 (一時停止, temporarily suspend, e.g. while abroad) — if you plan to return to Korea, 일시 정지 avoids the 위약금. Before 해지 is processed, expect to be asked for 본인 인증 and the remaining 약정 will be checked for a 위약금 amount.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I would like to terminate (the contract).' 실제: a formal service-cancellation opener. The ender -는데요 does heavy social work — it frames the cancellation as something you'd like the agent to help you with, rather than a command, keeping the tone cooperative and reducing resistance from retention-focused agents.

Said on the phone to a carrier's 해지 전담팀 (cancellation team) or at a store counter. Always 존댓말. Some carriers have dedicated 해지 retention teams that will offer discounts to keep you — be ready to say 그래도 해지하고 싶어요 ('I'd still like to cancel') if you want to proceed. In-person or ID verification is often required.

해지하려고 전화했어요 ('I called to cancel') is slightly more assertive — it states the purpose upfront and signals you've already decided, reducing the chance of being drawn into a retention pitch. The dividing line: 싶은데요 is open-ended and inviting; 하려고 전화했어요 is purposive and closed.
해지 신청하고 싶어요 (I'd like to apply to cancel), 해지 처리해 주세요 (please process the cancellation — stronger), 일시 정지하고 싶어요 (I'd like to suspend instead). 해지 without modifier means permanent termination.

Two traps: (1) 취소하고 싶어요 — 취소 cancels an order or booking (one-off transactions); for an ongoing contract the word is 해지. (2) 끝내고 싶어요 — 끝내다 ('to end/finish') is vague and rarely used for contracts; the industry term 해지 is required and immediately understood by staff.

mistakes: Saying 취소하고 싶어요 to cancel a contract.
취소 is for one-off orders/reservations. To end an ongoing contract/service, the word is 해지: 해지하고 싶은데요.
Saying 끝내고 싶어요.
끝내다 ('to finish') is vague for a contract. Use the specific term 해지하다 for canceling a phone/internet plan.
Forgetting 해지 may cost a 위약금.
Canceling before the 약정 ends usually incurs a 위약금 (penalty). Always ask 해지하면 위약금 얼마예요? If you'll return, consider 일시 정지 (suspend) instead.

english: How much is it per month?
usage: How much is it per month?
Polite; asking the monthly total for a plan
반말, to a friend comparing plans
월 요금 ('monthly fee') is the crisp set term
다 해서 한 달에 얼마 나와요?
All together, how much comes out per month?
다 해서 ('all in') asks the total including everything
examples: 기기값까지 하면 한 달에 얼마예요?
Including the phone, how much per month?
기기값 (device cost) is often spread across 24 months on the bill — confirm whether this is the plan price alone or the all-in total
할인 받으면 한 달에 얼마 나와요?
With the discount, how much comes out a month?
나오다 ('to come out') asks the real billed amount; 얼마예요? could be the list price — 나와요 always means what actually appears on the invoice
A: 이 요금제 한 달에 얼마예요? / B: 5만 5천 원인데요, 부가세 포함이에요. 기기값은 따로예요.
A: How much is this plan per month? / B: It's 55,000 won, VAT included. The phone cost is separate.
A/B exchange: the key caveat — 기기값은 따로예요 ('device cost is separate') is the most common source of sticker shock for newcomers; hearing this form prepares you for the response
nuance: 한 달에 얼마예요? is 한 달 ('one month') + 에 (the particle 'per/in') + 얼마예요? ('how much is it?'). The particle 에 here creates a 'per unit' meaning — 한 달에 = per month — the same pattern as 하루에 (per day), 일 년에 (per year). Default 존댓말 with staff. The natural variant using 나오다 ('to come out on the bill') — 한 달에 얼마 나와요? — is slightly more revealing because 나오다 specifically targets the amount that actually APPEARS on your monthly invoice, whereas 얼마예요? can refer to the list/advertised price before any add-ons. In practice, the gap between those two figures can be significant: the plan price, device installment (기기값 할부금), and VAT (부가세) may each appear as separate line items. Saying a bare 얼마예요? without 한 달에 risks being heard as asking the one-time phone price. Default 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Per one month, how much is it?' The 에 particle doing 'per' work is essential — without it 한 달 얼마예요? sounds incomplete. 실제: the core question for recurring costs; it targets the monthly charge of a plan but needs follow-up to confirm whether 기기값 and VAT are included.

Said at a carrier counter when comparing plans, on the phone with a carrier agent, or while browsing a plan comparison app. 존댓말 with staff. The most productive follow-up is 기기값 포함이에요? and 부가세 포함이에요? to determine whether the quoted figure is the true total.

한 달에 얼마 나와요? ('how much comes out a month?') is the bill-focused variant. The dividing line: 얼마예요? asks the listed/advertised price; 얼마 나와요? asks what actually appears on the invoice — these can differ by tens of thousands of won when 기기값 and 부가세 are added. Use 나와요? for the real cost check.
다 해서 한 달에 얼마예요? (all-in per month), 기기값 포함해서 얼마예요? (including device cost), 할인 적용하면 얼마예요? (with the discount applied). The 다 해서 version is the most comprehensive.

Two traps: (1) Dropping 에 and saying 한 달 얼마예요? — the particle 에 is required for the 'per' meaning; without it the phrase sounds incomplete or like you're naming the month. (2) Asking 매달 얼마 비용이에요? — 비용 is more formal/written ('cost/expense') and the phrasing is clunky; use the natural spoken form 한 달에 얼마예요? or 월 요금이 얼마예요?.

mistakes: Dropping 에 and saying 한 달 얼마예요?
'Per month' needs the particle 에: 한 달에 얼마예요? Without it the phrasing sounds incomplete.
Asking bare 얼마예요? for the monthly fee.
That can be heard as the one-time device price (기기값). Anchor it: 한 달에 얼마예요? for the recurring charge.
Saying 매달 얼마 비용이에요?
That's clunky and unidiomatic. Koreans ask 한 달에 얼마예요? or 한 달에 얼마 나와요? (the amount that 'comes out' on the bill).

usage: What do I need to sign up?
Polite; asking what to bring for enrollment
What do I need to sign up?
반말, to a friend who's done it
examples: 외국인인데 가입할 때 뭐 필요해요? 여권이요, 외국인 등록증이요?
I'm a foreigner — what do I need? Passport, or ARC?
Foreigners usually need 외국인 등록증 (ARC) if they have one; passport may work for short-stay tourists; flagging 외국인인데 immediately routes staff to the right document checklist
통장이나 카드도 필요해요?
Do I also need a bankbook or card?
통장 (bankbook) or 카드 is typically needed to set up 자동이체 (auto-debit); many contracts require it
A: 가입할 때 뭐 필요해요? / B: 외국인 등록증이랑 통장 있으면 돼요. 여권도 가능해요.
A: What do I need to sign up? / B: You need your ARC and a bank account. Passport also works.
A/B exchange: the typical staff answer for a foreigner — ARC or passport, plus bank account for auto-debit
nuance: 가입 (加入) is the act of enrolling as a subscriber — becoming a member of a carrier's service — and 할 때 ('when doing') + 뭐 ('what') + 필요해요? ('is needed?') asks what to bring. This is the practical preparation question before visiting a shop or filling out an online form. 필요하다 ('to be necessary') is an adjective in Korean, and its grammatical subject takes 이/가: 서류가 필요해요 ('documents are needed'), not 서류를. In casual questions 뭐 needed? drops the particle, which is fine. The key enrollment documents for foreigners: 외국인 등록증 (ARC, for residents), 여권 (passport, for tourists or those without ARC), 통장 or 카드 (for 자동이체 auto-pay setup). The contrast: 가입 is enrollment paperwork; 개통 is the line going live; 신청 is applying — you 가입 by submitting your ID and signing the contract, then the carrier 개통 your line. Saying 사인업할 때 using the English word is not Korean; use 가입할 때 exclusively.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'When signing up, what is necessary?' 실제: a practical checklist question asked before visiting a carrier shop to ensure you don't make a wasted trip. The answer almost always includes an ID card and a bank account or card for auto-debit.

Said on a preliminary phone call to the carrier, in a chat window, or asked of a Korean friend who has gone through the process. 존댓말 with staff. The single most important thing to say up front is 외국인인데요 — this immediately tells staff to give the foreigner-specific document list rather than assuming you have a 주민등록증 (Korean national ID).

필요한 서류 있어요? ('are there documents needed?') narrows the question specifically to paperwork rather than anything you might need (e.g., a payment method, a phone to register). The dividing line: 뭐 필요해요? is open-ended and catches all requirements; 필요한 서류 있어요? focuses only on documents. Use 뭐 필요해요? first, then 서류 있어요? as a follow-up.
외국인도 가입할 수 있어요? (can foreigners sign up?), 여권만 있으면 가입 돼요? (is just a passport enough?), 온라인으로 가입할 수 있어요? (can I sign up online?). 가입 is the fixed verb for all subscription enrollments.

Two traps: (1) 사인업할 때 — '사인업' is not a Korean word; use 가입할 때. (2) 서류를 필요해요 — 필요하다 is an adjective; its subject takes 이/가. Correct: 서류가 필요해요. The error 서류를 필요해요 ('I need documents' treating 필요 as a transitive verb) is one of the most common grammar mistakes at this level.

mistakes: Saying 사인업할 때 with the English 'sign up'.
사인업 isn't Korean. Use 가입 (enroll/join): 가입할 때 뭐 필요해요?
Confusing 가입 with 개통.
가입 is becoming a subscriber (the paperwork); 개통 is the line being switched on. Asking what's needed to 가입 is about ID and documents.
Using object 을 with 필요하다: 서류를 필요해요.
필요하다 ('to be needed') is an adjective; its subject takes 이/가, not 을. Correct: 서류가 필요해요 / 뭐가 필요해요?
